claim: Bicoid (Bcd) protein distributes in a concentration gradient that organizes the anterior/posterior axis of the Drosophila embryo.
source: Bicoid (Bcd) protein distributes in a concentration gradient that organizes the anterior/posterior axis of the Drosophila embryo.
evidence: This is a well-established finding supported by citations throughout the manuscript and is the foundational premise of the study.

claim: bcd RNA is sequestered at the anterior pole during oogenesis.
source: It has been understood that bcd RNA is sequestered at the anterior pole during oogenesis, is not translated until fertilization, and produces a protein gradient that functions in the syncytial blastoderm after 9–10 nuclear divisions.
evidence: This represents the prior understanding in the field, supported by historical citations.

claim: bcd RNA is not translated until fertilization (prior understanding).
source: It has been understood that bcd RNA is sequestered at the anterior pole during oogenesis, is not translated until fertilization, and produces a protein gradient that functions in the syncytial blastoderm after 9–10 nuclear divisions.
evidence: This is stated as prior understanding that the manuscript challenges.

claim: Bcd protein gradient functions in the syncytial blastoderm after 9-10 nuclear divisions (prior understanding).
source: It has been understood that bcd RNA is sequestered at the anterior pole during oogenesis, is not translated until fertilization, and produces a protein gradient that functions in the syncytial blastoderm after 9–10 nuclear divisions.
evidence: This represents the prior model that the manuscript revises.

claim: Technical issues limited the sensitivity of analysis of pre-syncytial blastoderm embryos.
source: However, technical issues limited the sensitivity of analysis of pre-syncytial blastoderm embryos and precluded studies of oocytes after stage 13.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation that motivated the development of new methods.

claim: Previous technical issues precluded studies of oocytes after stage 13.
source: However, technical issues limited the sensitivity of analysis of pre-syncytial blastoderm embryos and precluded studies of oocytes after stage 13.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in prior research that the current study addresses.

claim: Stage 14 oocytes make Bcd protein.
source: We developed methods to analyze stage 14 oocytes and pre-syncytial blastoderm embryos, and found that stage 14 oocytes make Bcd protein, that bcd RNA and Bcd protein distribute in matching concentration gradients in the interior of nuclear cycle 2–6 embryos, and that Bcd regulation of target gene expression is apparent at nuclear cycle 7, two cycles prior to syncytial blastoderm.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by antibody staining data shown in Figure 8.

claim: bcd RNA and Bcd protein distribute in matching concentration gradients in the interior of nuclear cycle 2-6 embryos.
source: We developed methods to analyze stage 14 oocytes and pre-syncytial blastoderm embryos, and found that stage 14 oocytes make Bcd protein, that bcd RNA and Bcd protein distribute in matching concentration gradients in the interior of nuclear cycle 2–6 embryos, and that Bcd regulation of target gene expression is apparent at nuclear cycle 7, two cycles prior to syncytial blastoderm.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in situ hybridization and antibody staining data shown in Figures 4-7.

claim: Bcd regulation of target gene expression is apparent at nuclear cycle 7.
source: We developed methods to analyze stage 14 oocytes and pre-syncytial blastoderm embryos, and found that stage 14 oocytes make Bcd protein, that bcd RNA and Bcd protein distribute in matching concentration gradients in the interior of nuclear cycle 2–6 embryos, and that Bcd regulation of target gene expression is apparent at nuclear cycle 7, two cycles prior to syncytial blastoderm.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by Kr expression data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Bcd regulation of target gene expression occurs two cycles prior to syncytial blastoderm.
source: We developed methods to analyze stage 14 oocytes and pre-syncytial blastoderm embryos, and found that stage 14 oocytes make Bcd protein, that bcd RNA and Bcd protein distribute in matching concentration gradients in the interior of nuclear cycle 2–6 embryos, and that Bcd regulation of target gene expression is apparent at nuclear cycle 7, two cycles prior to syncytial blastoderm.
evidence: This is derived from the finding that regulation occurs at nc7, while syncytial blastoderm begins at nc9.

claim: The discovery of the Bicoid protein concentration gradient established the existence and functional importance of a morphogen gradient for the first time.
source: The discovery of the concentration gradient of Bicoid (Bcd) protein in the early Drosophila embryo established the existence and functional importance of a morphogen gradient for the first time (Driever and Nusslein-Volhard, 1988a, 1988b; Frigerio et al., 1986); it was a watershed moment in developmental biology.
evidence: This is a historical statement supported by citations to foundational papers.

claim: Bcd protein is present at the cortex of pre-cellular, syncytial blastoderm embryos.
source: These and subsequent studies showed that Bcd protein is present at the cortex of pre-cellular, syncytial blastoderm embryos, with levels that are highest at the anterior end and that decline exponentially toward the posterior (Driever and Nusslein-Volhard, 1988b; Gregor et al., 2007; Spirov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Bcd protein levels are highest at the anterior end and decline exponentially toward the posterior.
source: These and subsequent studies showed that Bcd protein is present at the cortex of pre-cellular, syncytial blastoderm embryos, with levels that are highest at the anterior end and that decline exponentially toward the posterior (Driever and Nusslein-Volhard, 1988b; Gregor et al., 2007; Spirov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: bcd mRNA is concentrated in the anterior cytoplasm of stage 13 oocytes.
source: Although bcd mRNA is concentrated in the anterior cytoplasm of stage 13 oocytes and of embryos immediately after egg laying (Berleth et al., 1988; Frigerio et al., 1986; Riechmann and Ephrussi, 2004), its distribution extends more posteriorly in the embryo at syncytial blastoderm stages (Berleth et al., 1988; Frigerio et al., 1986; Spirov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: bcd mRNA is concentrated in the anterior cytoplasm of embryos immediately after egg laying.
source: Although bcd mRNA is concentrated in the anterior cytoplasm of stage 13 oocytes and of embryos immediately after egg laying (Berleth et al., 1988; Frigerio et al., 1986; Riechmann and Ephrussi, 2004), its distribution extends more posteriorly in the embryo at syncytial blastoderm stages (Berleth et al., 1988; Frigerio et al., 1986; Spirov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: bcd mRNA distribution extends more posteriorly in the embryo at syncytial blastoderm stages.
source: Although bcd mRNA is concentrated in the anterior cytoplasm of stage 13 oocytes and of embryos immediately after egg laying (Berleth et al., 1988; Frigerio et al., 1986; Riechmann and Ephrussi, 2004), its distribution extends more posteriorly in the embryo at syncytial blastoderm stages (Berleth et al., 1988; Frigerio et al., 1986; Spirov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is a dispute about whether the Bcd protein gradient forms by passive diffusion following synthesis at anterior locations or is produced in place by the bcd mRNA concentration gradient.
source: Whether the protein gradient forms by passive diffusion following synthesis of Bcd protein at more anterior locations (Gregor et al., 2007; Little et al., 2011), or is produced in place by the bcd mRNA concentration gradient is in dispute (Fahmy et al., 2014; Spirov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to conflicting models in the literature.

claim: After fertilization, nuclei divide rapidly and synchronously eight times in the interior of the embryo.
source: After fertilization, nuclei divide rapidly and synchronously eight times in the interior of the embryo, moving outward in a choreographed sequence that places them simultaneously at the surface at nuclear cycle 9 (nc9).
evidence: This is a well-established developmental fact.

claim: Nuclei move outward in a choreographed sequence that places them simultaneously at the surface at nuclear cycle 9.
source: After fertilization, nuclei divide rapidly and synchronously eight times in the interior of the embryo, moving outward in a choreographed sequence that places them simultaneously at the surface at nuclear cycle 9 (nc9).
evidence: This is a well-established developmental fact.

claim: The five division cycles following nuclear cycle 9 delineate the syncytial blastoderm stages nc10-nc14.
source: The five division cycles that follow delineate the syncytial blastoderm stages nc10-nc14.
evidence: This is a well-established developmental fact.

claim: Nuclear divisions cease at nc14.
source: Nuclear divisions cease at nc14, whereupon the nuclei begin to individuate into single cells and gastrulation ensues.
evidence: This is a well-established developmental fact.

claim: At nc14, nuclei begin to individuate into single cells and gastrulation ensues.
source: Nuclear divisions cease at nc14, whereupon the nuclei begin to individuate into single cells and gastrulation ensues.
evidence: This is a well-established developmental fact.

claim: The zygotic genome is transcriptionally activated during the syncytial blastoderm period.
source: Various measures, including in situ hybridization (Erickson and Cline, 1993; Pritchard and Schubiger, 1996), RT-PCR (Harrison et al., 2010), genome array hybridization (De Renzis et al., 2007; Little et al., 2011; Lu et al., 2009), RNA seq (Lott et al., 2011), DNA footprinting (Harrison et al., 2010), chromatin profiling (Harrison et al., 2011) and ChIP-seq (Blythe and Wieschaus, 2015), show that the zygotic genome is transcriptionally activated during the syncytial blastoderm period.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to various molecular studies.

claim: Oogenesis provides the Drosophila egg with a rich dowry of mRNA that is essential to the development of the early, pre-cellular embryo.
source: Oogenesis provides the Drosophila egg with a rich dowry of mRNA that is essential to the development of the early, pre-cellular embryo, and for a number of reasons, the period that precedes the maternal-to-zygotic transition has been considered to depend only on maternal stores and to be independent of the zygotic genome.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about Drosophila development.

claim: The period that precedes the maternal-to-zygotic transition has been considered to depend only on maternal stores and to be independent of the zygotic genome.
source: Oogenesis provides the Drosophila egg with a rich dowry of mRNA that is essential to the development of the early, pre-cellular embryo, and for a number of reasons, the period that precedes the maternal-to-zygotic transition has been considered to depend only on maternal stores and to be independent of the zygotic genome.
evidence: This represents the prior understanding that the manuscript challenges.

claim: Early nuclear divisions are so rapid (9.6 min) that productive gene expression has been deemed impossible.
source: One, the early nuclear divisions are so rapid (9.6 min) that productive gene expression has been deemed impossible.
evidence: This is stated as a reason for the prior belief that early embryos lack zygotic transcription.

claim: Molecular analyses of transcriptional activity have almost universally failed to detect RNA synthesis at pre-syncytial blastoderm stages.
source: Two, molecular analyses of transcriptional activity have almost universally failed to detect RNA synthesis at pre-syncytial blastoderm stages, even as the sensitivity of the detection methods has increased.
evidence: This is stated as a reason for the prior belief, based on negative findings.

claim: Comprehensive genetic screens for mutants defective in early development identified many genes that are required maternally.
source: Three, comprehensive genetic screens for mutants defective in early development identified many genes that are required maternally, but found no evidence for genes that must be active in the zygote prior to cellularization at nc14 (Luschnig et al., 2004; Merrill et al., 1988; Perrimon et al., 1984; Schupbach and Wieschaus, 1989, 1991; 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic screens.

claim: Comprehensive genetic screens found no evidence for genes that must be active in the zygote prior to cellularization at nc14.
source: Three, comprehensive genetic screens for mutants defective in early development identified many genes that are required maternally, but found no evidence for genes that must be active in the zygote prior to cellularization at nc14 (Luschnig et al., 2004; Merrill et al., 1988; Perrimon et al., 1984; Schupbach and Wieschaus, 1989, 1991; 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic screens.

claim: Drosophila embryos are heavily populated with yolk and glycogen granules that impede histological studies.
source: Drosophila embryos are heavily populated with yolk and glycogen granules that impede histological studies, and have few obvious morphological features that can be evaluated for dependence on genotype.
evidence: This is stated as a technical challenge that has limited prior studies.

claim: Drosophila embryos have few obvious morphological features that can be evaluated for dependence on genotype.
source: Drosophila embryos are heavily populated with yolk and glycogen granules that impede histological studies, and have few obvious morphological features that can be evaluated for dependence on genotype.
evidence: This is stated as a technical challenge that has limited prior studies.

claim: The earliest reported zygotic expression obtained by in situ hybridization is at nc8 for the gene sis-A.
source: The earliest reported zygotic expression obtained by in situ hybridization is at nc8 for the gene sis-A (Erickson and Cline, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Evidence for earlier gene expression (β-galactosidase activity in nc4 embryos) was reported for a transgene construct that carried the lacZ gene regulated by a FTZ-F2 enhancer fragment.
source: Evidence for earlier gene expression (β-galactosidase activity in nc4 embryos) was reported for a transgene construct that carried the lacZ gene regulated by a FTZ-F2 enhancer fragment (Brown et al., 1991).

claim: A mutant phenotype was identified in en nc2-3 embryos.

claim: Development of the early embryo is not entirely pre-programmed.
source: These findings show that development of the early embryo is not entirely pre-programmed and that the processes that orchestrate the early stages are actively and directly regulated.

claim: The processes that orchestrate the early stages are actively and directly regulated.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: In situ hybridization can detect sites of nascent transcript production as points of staining or fluorescence.
source: In situ hybridization can detect sites of nascent transcript production as points of staining or fluorescence (Femino et al., 1998; Shermoen and O'Farrell, 1991), and the nc10-13 embryos we analyzed had bright dots in most or all nuclei in the 'Kr band'.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous methodological studies.

claim: nc10-13 embryos had bright dots in most or all nuclei in the 'Kr band'.

claim: The fraction of nuclei with dots was lower in nc7-9 embryos.

claim: Most of the nuclei with dots in nc7-9 embryos were in the central region where the Kr band forms.

claim: The position of the Kr band, but not the number of Kr dots, was sensitive to maternal bcd gene dosage.
source: The position of the Kr band, but not the number of Kr dots, was sensitive to maternal bcd gene dosage: in nc12 embryos, it was at 43–64% embryo length (from anterior end) if mothers were wild type (had two bcd copies) and 54–75% if mothers had six.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: In nc12 embryos, the Kr band was at 43-64% embryo length (from anterior end) if mothers were wild type (had two bcd copies).

claim: Nuclear dots increased in number and brightness as the cycle progressed.

claim: Nuclear dots reached peak brightness at late interphase-early prophase.
source: The dots were absent from early interphase nuclei, but increased in number and brightness as the cycle progressed, and they reached peak brightness at late interphase-early prophase (Figure 2A,B).

claim: The level of fluorescence in the cytoplasm increased during the nuclear cycles.
source: The level of fluorescence in the cytoplasm also increased during the nuclear cycles.

claim: Both nuclear dot and cytoplasmic fluorescence was higher at nc11 relative to nc9.

claim: The increase in dot brightness during the nuclear cycle suggests that the in situ hybridization signal is proportional to the quantity (number and length) of transcripts.

claim: The Kr gene is at the tip of 2R (polytene band 60F5).
source: Because the Kr gene is at the tip of 2R (polytene band 60F5), this result suggests that nuclei are polarized prior to their arrival at the cortex and it is consistent with the conclusion that the nuclear dots mark sites of Kr transcription.

claim: Nuclei are polarized prior to their arrival at the cortex.

claim: The nuclear dots mark sites of Kr transcription.

claim: Staining by the anti-Bcd antibody was apparent and fluorescent punctae were visible in nuclei of the nc6 exu mutant embryo.

claim: Bcd protein was present in the interior of mutant pre-syncytial blastoderm embryos, although its distribution was apparently more uniform than WT.

claim: bcd RNA was concentrated at the anterior end of pre-cellular stages in patterns that were similar to Bcd protein.

claim: bcd RNA was concentrated at the anterior end of nc2 embryos.

claim: In nc4 embryos, bcd RNA formed a plume that extended posteriorly in the embryo interior.

evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6.

claim: bcd RNA was predominantly anterior and cortical in embryos at stages nc8 and older.
source: It was predominantly anterior and cortical in embryos at stages nc8 and older.

claim: Images of bcd RNA in syncytial blastoderm stage embryos are consistent with previous reports.
source: These images of bcd RNA in syncytial blastoderm stage embryos are consistent with previous reports (Little et al., 2011; Spirov et al., 2009).

claim: The bcd RNA was tightly restricted at the anterior end at nc1.

claim: At nc3, bcd RNA was distributed in an internal plume that had distinct contours and dorsal/ventral asymmetries.
source: Higher resolution examination of the anatomy of the RNA distribution at nc1 and nc3 stages (Figure 7) revealed that the RNA was tightly restricted at the anterior end at nc1, but at nc3 was distributed in an internal plume that had distinct contours and dorsal/ventral asymmetries.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The posterior extent of the bcd RNA plume was greatest at nc4.
source: The posterior extent of the plume was greatest at nc4, and was not as great at nc5 and nc6.

claim: The posterior extent of the bcd RNA plume was not as great at nc5 and nc6 as at nc4.
source: The posterior extent of the plume was greatest at nc4, and was not as great at nc5 and nc6.

claim: Bcd protein was detected in unfertilized eggs.
source: Although Bcd protein was detected in unfertilized eggs, the assumption was made that stage 14 oocytes have anterior-localized RNA but no Bcd protein, and that the protein in unfertilized eggs was produced in conjunction with egg activation and egg laying.

claim: The assumption was made that stage 14 oocytes have anterior-localized RNA but no Bcd protein (prior understanding).
source: Although Bcd protein was detected in unfertilized eggs, the assumption was made that stage 14 oocytes have anterior-localized RNA but no Bcd protein, and that the protein in unfertilized eggs was produced in conjunction with egg activation and egg laying.
evidence: This is stated as prior understanding that the manuscript challenges.

claim: The assumption was made that the protein in unfertilized eggs was produced in conjunction with egg activation and egg laying (prior understanding).
source: Although Bcd protein was detected in unfertilized eggs, the assumption was made that stage 14 oocytes have anterior-localized RNA but no Bcd protein, and that the protein in unfertilized eggs was produced in conjunction with egg activation and egg laying.
evidence: This is stated as prior understanding that the manuscript challenges.

claim: Previous studies of stage 14 oocytes have been limited to in situ hybridization analysis of ovarian sections.
source: However, because there have not been suitable methods for fixation and preparation, previous studies of stage 14 oocytes have been limited to in situ hybridization analysis of ovarian sections (Frigerio et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and explains the gap in prior research.

claim: Stage 14 oocytes have vitelline membrane and chorion layers that reduce permeability.
source: In contrast to younger oocytes, stage 14 oocytes have vitelline membrane and chorion layers that reduce permeability, but they are sensitive to hypochlorite and organic solvent treatments that are resisted by the fully formed vitelline membrane and chorion layers of subsequent stages.

claim: Stage 14 oocytes are sensitive to hypochlorite and organic solvent treatments that are resisted by the fully formed vitelline membrane and chorion layers of subsequent stages.
source: In contrast to younger oocytes, stage 14 oocytes have vitelline membrane and chorion layers that reduce permeability, but they are sensitive to hypochlorite and organic solvent treatments that are resisted by the fully formed vitelline membrane and chorion layers of subsequent stages.
evidence: This is stated as a technical property that enabled the development of new methods.

claim: Significant levels of Bcd protein are present in early nc1 embryos and unfertilized eggs.
source: We sought methods to examine bcd RNA and protein in stage 14 oocytes because our analysis revealed that significant levels of Bcd protein are present in early nc1 embryos and unfertilized eggs (Figure 8).

claim: Staining with anti-Bcd antibody did not detect Bcd protein in stage 13 or stage 14a-b oocytes.
source: Staining with anti-Bcd antibody did not detect Bcd protein in stage 13 (not shown) or stage 14a–b oocytes (Figure 8H,I), but detected Bcd protein in stage 14c (not shown) and 14d oocytes (Figure 8L).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Anti-Bcd antibody detected Bcd protein in stage 14c and 14d oocytes.
source: Staining with anti-Bcd antibody did not detect Bcd protein in stage 13 (not shown) or stage 14a–b oocytes (Figure 8H,I), but detected Bcd protein in stage 14c (not shown) and 14d oocytes (Figure 8L).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Bcd protein was present in a tightly delineated band that follows the contours of the oblique concavity at the oocyte's anterior end.
source: Bcd protein was present in a tightly delineated band that follows the contours of the oblique concavity at the oocyte's anterior end.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: In situ hybridization detected bcd RNA in a band that follows the anterior concavity of stage 14 oocytes.
source: In situ hybridization also detected bcd RNA in a band that follows the anterior concavity of stage 14 oocytes.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 8.

claim: bcd RNA distribution in stage 14 oocytes was similar to the Bcd protein except that it was detected at stage 12, 13, and all periods of stage 14.
source: This RNA distribution was similar to the Bcd protein except that in contrast to the protein, it was detected at stage 12 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) and 13 (not shown) and all periods of stage 14.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The translation block that inhibits Bcd protein production is relieved prior to fertilization and egg activation.
source: These results show that the translation block that inhibits Bcd protein production is relieved prior to fertilization and egg activation, and shows that Bcd protein is produced and is present precisely at the site where bcd RNA is sequestered.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Bcd protein is present in late stage 14 oocytes.

claim: Bcd protein is produced and is present precisely at the site where bcd RNA is sequestered.
source: These results show that the translation block that inhibits Bcd protein production is relieved prior to fertilization and egg activation, and shows that Bcd protein is produced and is present precisely at the site where bcd RNA is sequestered.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that Bcd protein and bcd RNA have matching distributions in stage 14 oocytes.

claim: The cortical nuclei at the surface of late syncytial blastoderm embryos have apical-basal polarity that is manifested in the organization of their chromosomes.
source: The cortical nuclei at the surface of late syncytial blastoderm embryos have apical-basal polarity that is manifested in the organization of their chromosomes.
evidence: This is a known fact supported by the citation that follows.

claim: The centromeric regions of the chromosomes coalesce to form a chromocenter that is at the most apical aspect of the nuclei.
source: Whereas the centromeric regions of the chromosomes coalesce to form a chromocenter that is at the most apical aspect of the nuclei, the telomeres congregate basally (Marshall et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The telomeres congregate basally in cortical nuclei at the surface of late syncytial blastoderm embryos.
source: Whereas the centromeric regions of the chromosomes coalesce to form a chromocenter that is at the most apical aspect of the nuclei, the telomeres congregate basally (Marshall et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Chromosome organization in nuclei at earlier, pre-syncytial blastoderm stages has not been examined previously.
source: Chromosome organization in nuclei at earlier, pre-syncytial blastoderm stages has not been examined previously.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in prior research.

claim: The nascent transcripts at the Kr gene are at the basal regions of nc7 and nc8 nuclei.
source: Our in situ hybridization experiments located nascent transcripts at the Kr gene, which is situated just proximal to the telomere of chromosome 2R, and analysis of serial optical sections revealed that the nascent transcripts are at the basal regions of nc7 and nc8 nuclei (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Nuclei in the interior of the embryo are organized and polarized with respect to the cortex.
source: These nuclei are approximately 34 μm and 22 μm, respectively, from the embryo surface, indicating that nuclei in the interior of the embryo are organized and polarized with respect to the cortex.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nascent transcripts are at the basal regions of interior nuclei.

claim: The idea that internal chromosome organization is related to gene expression is consistent with the finding that nc7-8 nuclei are transcriptionally active.
source: The idea that internal chromosome organization is related to gene expression (Marshall et al., 1996) is consistent with our finding that these nuclei are transcriptionally active.
evidence: This is an inference connecting a cited idea to the current findings.

claim: Nuclear divisions in the pre-syncytial blastoderm embryo are precisely synchronized even as the nuclei move to collectively occupy larger volumes of the embryo at later nuclear cycles.
source: Nuclear divisions in the pre-syncytial blastoderm embryo are precisely synchronized even as the nuclei move to collectively occupy larger volumes of the embryo at later nuclear cycles, and the choreography they follow as they move to the cortex is highly reproducible.
evidence: This is a known fact about early embryo development.

claim: The choreography nuclei follow as they move to the cortex is highly reproducible.
source: Nuclear divisions in the pre-syncytial blastoderm embryo are precisely synchronized even as the nuclei move to collectively occupy larger volumes of the embryo at later nuclear cycles, and the choreography they follow as they move to the cortex is highly reproducible.
evidence: This is a known fact about early embryo development.

claim: The apical-basal polarity of nuclei is not a consequence of short-range interactions with the cortex.
source: Our finding that nuclei are oriented prior to their arrival at the cortex indicates that their apical-basal polarity is not a consequence of short-range interactions with the cortex, and suggests that a global system of structural organization and regulation exists in the early embryo.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that interior nuclei are already polarized.

claim: A global system of structural organization and regulation exists in the early embryo.
source: Our finding that nuclei are oriented prior to their arrival at the cortex indicates that their apical-basal polarity is not a consequence of short-range interactions with the cortex, and suggests that a global system of structural organization and regulation exists in the early embryo.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of nuclear polarity in the interior.

claim: The Bcd concentration gradient is generated from mRNA that is made by nurse cells and is transported to the oocyte where it is sequestered in an inactive state at the anterior end.
source: The Bcd concentration gradient is generated from mRNA that is made by nurse cells and is transported to the oocyte where it is sequestered in an inactive state at the anterior end (Frigerio et al., 1986).
evidence: This is a well-established fact supported by a citation.

claim: Previous studies reported that Bcd protein was absent from stage 13 oocytes but present in embryos and unfertilized eggs.
source: Previous studies reported that Bcd protein was absent from stage 13 oocytes but present in embryos and unfertilized eggs (Driever and Nusslein-Volhard, 1988b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The current model is that translation of Bcd protein begins at egg activation.
source: Although stage 14 oocytes were not examined, the assumption that Bcd protein is also absent from stage 14 oocytes was the basis for the current model that translation of Bcd protein begins at egg activation.
evidence: This is stated as the prior model that the manuscript revises.

claim: The finding that Bcd protein is made in late stage oocytes prior to activation and fertilization revises the current model.
source: Our finding that Bcd protein is made in late stage oocytes prior to activation and fertilization (Figure 8) revises this model, but does not fundamentally change it.
evidence: This is stated as a revision to the prior model based on the current findings.

claim: The distribution of Bcd protein in stage 14c and 14d oocytes is consistent with the idea that Bcd protein is made by mRNA that was localized to the anterior end.
source: The distribution of Bcd protein in stage 14c and 14d oocytes is consistent with the idea that Bcd protein is made by mRNA that was localized to the anterior end.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Bcd protein and bcd RNA have matching distributions.

claim: The production of Bcd in the oocyte raises the question whether Bcd protein is made only in the oocyte and not in the embryo.
source: Its production in the oocyte raises the question whether Bcd protein is made only in the oocyte and not in the embryo, but this seems unlikely because the level of staining by α-Bcd antibody increased during the pre-cellular cycles (Figure 4).
evidence: This is speculation about the implications of the findings.

claim: It seems unlikely that Bcd protein is made only in the oocyte and not in the embryo because the level of staining by α-Bcd antibody increased during the pre-cellular cycles.
source: Its production in the oocyte raises the question whether Bcd protein is made only in the oocyte and not in the embryo, but this seems unlikely because the level of staining by α-Bcd antibody increased during the pre-cellular cycles (Figure 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of increasing Bcd levels in early embryos.

claim: One model posits that the Bcd protein gradient is a direct consequence of the location of bcd mRNA.
source: One is based on the observation that both bcd mRNA and Bcd protein distribute in concentration gradients at syncytial blastoderm stages (nc9-14), and because of the spatial relationship between these distributions, it posits that the Bcd protein gradient is a direct consequence of the location of bcd mRNA (Fahmy et al., 2014; Spirov et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a model from the literature supported by citations.

claim: One model does not require or invoke a role for protein diffusion, but proposes that a process of directed and regulated transport produces a concentration gradient of bcd mRNA that precedes and generates the Bcd protein gradient.
source: This model does not require or invoke a role for protein diffusion, but proposes instead that a process of directed and regulated transport produces a concentration gradient of bcd mRNA that precedes and generates the Bcd protein gradient.
evidence: This is a model from the literature.

claim: The second model proposes a major role for Bcd protein diffusion.
source: The second model also involves a gradient of bcd RNA, but because the bcd RNA was not observed to extend as far posteriorly as Bcd protein, it proposes a major role for Bcd protein diffusion (Little et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a model from the literature supported by a citation.

claim: bcd RNA and Bcd protein formed similar distributions in the interior of pre-syncytial blastoderm embryos.
source: We observed that bcd RNA and Bcd protein formed similar distributions in the interior of pre-syncytial blastoderm embryos (Figures 4–7).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 4-7.

claim: The approximate match between the RNA and protein patterns remained constant during pre-syncytial blastoderm stages.
source: Although these distributions were constantly changing, the approximate match between the RNA and protein patterns remained constant.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of similar distributions at multiple stages.

claim: The RNA and protein were tightly concentrated at the anterior end of stage 14 oocytes, broader in nc1 embryos, and formed a graded internal plume that extended the farthest toward the posterior in nc3-4 embryos.
source: The RNA and protein were tightly concentrated at the anterior end of stage 14 oocytes, broader in nc1 embryos, and formed a graded internal plume that extended the farthest toward the posterior in nc3-4 embryos.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 4-8.

claim: The bcd RNA/protein plume had complex geometries that were not radially symmetric.
source: The plume had complex geometries that were not radially symmetric, but after nc6-7, the internal plume was no longer visible and most of the bcd RNA and protein was near or at the cortex.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 4-7.

claim: After nc6-7, the internal plume was no longer visible and most of the bcd RNA and protein was near or at the cortex.
source: The plume had complex geometries that were not radially symmetric, but after nc6-7, the internal plume was no longer visible and most of the bcd RNA and protein was near or at the cortex.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 4-7.

claim: The cortical distributions of bcd RNA and protein were radially symmetric.
source: The cortical distributions were radially symmetric.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 4-7.

claim: The mechanisms that generate the bcd RNA and protein distributions are not known.
source: The mechanisms that generate these distributions are not known, but because the patterns of bcd RNA and protein are so similar, we suggest that the mechanisms are probably related.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in understanding.

claim: The mechanisms that generate bcd RNA and protein distributions are probably related.
source: The mechanisms that generate these distributions are not known, but because the patterns of bcd RNA and protein are so similar, we suggest that the mechanisms are probably related.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of similar distributions.

claim: The complex and well-defined shapes and the rapidity with which the distributions form and change would seem to be incompatible with passive diffusion.
source: Although these mechanisms cannot be deduced from the geometries of the distributions, the complex and well-defined shapes and the rapidity with which the distributions form and change would seem to be incompatible with passive diffusion.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed characteristics of the distributions.

claim: The bcd RNA and Bcd protein distributions in the pre-cellular embryo reveal two distinct concentration gradients – one in the embryo interior that forms between nc1 and nc6, and a second one that forms later at the embryo cortex.
source: The bcd RNA and Bcd protein distributions we observed in the pre-cellular embryo reveal two distinct concentration gradients – one in the embryo interior that forms between nc1 and nc6, and a second one that forms later at the embryo cortex.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the observations from the data.

claim: The bcd RNA and Bcd protein of the early, first gradient contribute to the second gradient.
source: We assume that the bcd RNA and Bcd protein of the early, first gradient contribute to the second, and therefore call this a two-step model.
evidence: This is an assumption made by the authors to explain the observations.

claim: The two-step model contrasts with the models that have been proposed previously in which the dispersion of protein (and RNA) from the anterior pole is continuous during both the pre-syncytial blastoderm and syncytial blastoderm stages.
source: This model contrasts with the models that have been proposed previously in which the dispersion of protein (and RNA) from the anterior pole is continuous during both the pre-syncytial blastoderm and syncytial blastoderm stages (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a comparison of the new model to previous models, illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: The two-step model is presumably generated by motor-driven directed movement.
source: Although the two-step model is presumably generated by motor-driven directed movement, the high yolk content of the embryo cytoplasm has impeded analysis of its cytoskeletal elements.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the two-step model.

claim: The high yolk content of the embryo cytoplasm has impeded analysis of its cytoskeletal elements.
source: Although the two-step model is presumably generated by motor-driven directed movement, the high yolk content of the embryo cytoplasm has impeded analysis of its cytoskeletal elements.
evidence: This is stated as a technical challenge.

claim: Several studies have reported microtubule networks in the pre-syncytial embryo.
source: However, several studies have reported microtubule networks in the pre-syncytial embryo (Fahmy et al., 2014; Karr and Alberts, 1986) and threads of microtubules up to 50 μm long extending from the cortex into the interior at syncytial blastoderm stages (Fahmy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Threads of microtubules up to 50 μm long extend from the cortex into the interior at syncytial blastoderm stages.
source: However, several studies have reported microtubule networks in the pre-syncytial embryo (Fahmy et al., 2014; Karr and Alberts, 1986) and threads of microtubules up to 50 μm long extending from the cortex into the interior at syncytial blastoderm stages (Fahmy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Microtubule networks offer a possible mechanism that might transport particles of bcd RNA and protein posteriorly to form the internal plume in pre-nc6 embryos.
source: These networks offer a possible mechanism that might transport particles of bcd RNA (Fahmy et al., 2014; Spirov et al., 2009) and protein posteriorly to form the internal plume in pre-nc6 embryos (Figures 4–7), and to re-distribute bcd RNA and protein to the cortex at blastoderm stages.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism based on the existence of microtubule networks.

claim: Microtubule networks might re-distribute bcd RNA and protein to the cortex at blastoderm stages.
source: These networks offer a possible mechanism that might transport particles of bcd RNA (Fahmy et al., 2014; Spirov et al., 2009) and protein posteriorly to form the internal plume in pre-nc6 embryos (Figures 4–7), and to re-distribute bcd RNA and protein to the cortex at blastoderm stages.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism based on the existence of microtubule networks.

claim: Transcription initiates at Kr as early as nc7.
source: Our analysis of Kr expression revealed that transcription initiates as early as nc7 (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The internal nuclei with Kr transcripts were at the approximate position along the anterior/posterior axis where older, syncytial blastoderm embryos have robust Kr expression.
source: Although the number of nuclei with nascent Kr transcripts was small, the internal nuclei with transcripts were at the approximate position along the anterior/posterior axis where older, syncytial blastoderm embryos have robust Kr expression, and this position was influenced by the level of Bcd protein in a similar way as the later, cortical expression.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The position of Kr expression in nc7 nuclei was influenced by the level of Bcd protein in a similar way as the later, cortical expression.
source: Although the number of nuclei with nascent Kr transcripts was small, the internal nuclei with transcripts were at the approximate position along the anterior/posterior axis where older, syncytial blastoderm embryos have robust Kr expression, and this position was influenced by the level of Bcd protein in a similar way as the later, cortical expression.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A concentration gradient of nuclear Bcd protein was detected at the nc6 stage, when the embryo has just 32 nuclei that are deep in the interior.
source: We also detected a concentration gradient of nuclear Bcd protein at the nc6 stage, when the embryo has just 32 nuclei that are deep in the interior (Figure 5), and observed that the both the internal and cortical Bcd gradients as well as both internal and cortical Kr expression were abnormal in exu and stau mutant embryos (Figures 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Both the internal and cortical Bcd gradients as well as both internal and cortical Kr expression were abnormal in exu and stau mutant embryos.
source: We also detected a concentration gradient of nuclear Bcd protein at the nc6 stage, when the embryo has just 32 nuclei that are deep in the interior (Figure 5), and observed that the both the internal and cortical Bcd gradients as well as both internal and cortical Kr expression were abnormal in exu and stau mutant embryos (Figures 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Bcd regulates Kr in nuclei that are far from the cortex.
source: These results show that Bcd regulates Kr in nuclei that are far from the cortex, and importantly, that the internal plume of Bcd protein is a functional distribution.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of Kr expression in interior nuclei and its dependence on Bcd levels.

claim: The internal plume of Bcd protein is a functional distribution.
source: These results show that Bcd regulates Kr in nuclei that are far from the cortex, and importantly, that the internal plume of Bcd protein is a functional distribution.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Kr expression in interior nuclei depends on Bcd.

claim: It is the pre-syncytial blastoderm, internal Bcd gradient that regulates gap gene expression and organizes the embryo's anterior/posterior axis.
source: These findings therefore establish that it is the pre-syncytial blastoderm, internal Bcd gradient that regulates gap gene expression and organizes the embryo's anterior/posterior axis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings about early Kr expression and its regulation by Bcd.

claim: It is most likely that the cortical gradient derives from the earlier distribution and therefore that it reflects the outputs of the pre-syncytial blastoderm, internal gradient.
source: Although these findings do not imply what the role of the subsequent cortical Bcd gradient in the syncytial blastoderm stages Bcd gradient might be, it is most likely that the cortical gradient derives from the earlier distribution and therefore that it reflects the outputs of the pre-syncytial blastoderm, internal gradient.
evidence: This is speculation about the relationship between the two gradients.

claim: Morphogens such as Hedgehog, Wingless, Decapentaplegic, and Fibroblast growth factor distribute in concentration gradients across fields of cells in the tissues of developing animals.
source: Morphogens such as Hedgehog, Wingless, Decapentaplegic, and Fibroblast growth factor distribute in concentration gradients across fields of cells in the tissues of developing animals.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about morphogen gradients.

claim: Morphogen distributions are generated by transport along actin-based cytonemes.
source: Their distributions are generated by transport along actin-based cytonemes (Roy, 2011 #56 and reviewed in Kornberg, 2014) and direct exchange between producing and receiving cells at morphogenetic synapses where release and uptake of secreted proteins is regulated (Roy, 2014 #57 and reviewed in Kornberg and Roy, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Direct exchange between producing and receiving cells occurs at morphogenetic synapses where release and uptake of secreted proteins is regulated.
source: Their distributions are generated by transport along actin-based cytonemes (Roy, 2011 #56 and reviewed in Kornberg, 2014) and direct exchange between producing and receiving cells at morphogenetic synapses where release and uptake of secreted proteins is regulated (Roy, 2014 #57 and reviewed in Kornberg and Roy, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Neither the Bcd gradient nor cytoneme-mediated morphogen gradients appear to be dependent on passive diffusion.
source: The generation of the Bcd concentration gradients in the pre-cellular embryo would appear to have little in common with the gradients that form by cytoneme-mediated dispersion across fields of cells, but we pose the question whether they do. Neither appears to be dependent on passive diffusion and both appear to involve dispersion along cytoskeletal cables.
evidence: This is speculation comparing the Bcd gradient to other morphogen gradients.

claim: Both the Bcd gradient and cytoneme-mediated morphogen gradients appear to involve dispersion along cytoskeletal cables.
source: The generation of the Bcd concentration gradients in the pre-cellular embryo would appear to have little in common with the gradients that form by cytoneme-mediated dispersion across fields of cells, but we pose the question whether they do. Neither appears to be dependent on passive diffusion and both appear to involve dispersion along cytoskeletal cables.
evidence: This is speculation comparing the Bcd gradient to other morphogen gradients.

claim: The critical attribute that the Bcd gradient mechanism and cytoneme-mediated dispersion share is that they provide ways to regulate movement in space and time.
source: The critical attribute that these mechanisms share is that they provide ways to regulate movement in space and time.
evidence: This is speculation about the common feature of these mechanisms.
